original_title: US Consumers Pay $2,100 More Per Year in Tariff Costs Per Household

sources.title: Where We Stand: Fiscal, Economic, and Distributional Effects of All U.S. Tariffs Enacted in 2025 Through April
sources.access_notes: The model distinguishes the April 2 tariffs from all tariffs then in effect and estimates purchasing-power effects, not a realized household bill.

supported_facts.fact: Yale Budget Lab estimated an average household purchasing-power loss of about $2,100 from the April 2 tariff package; its estimate for all tariffs then in effect was about $3,800. These are modeled impacts, not observed payments.

unsupported_original_claims: Households had already paid $2,100 more per year in realized tariff costs.
The $2,100 estimate covered all tariffs then in effect.
Economists unanimously confirmed the stated consumer-incidence claim.
The source establishes the distributional claim about lower-income households in the form stated.
access_notes: The estimate is modeled purchasing-power impact from the April 2 tariffs alone; the all-tariff estimate was about $3,800. The April 10 record date follows the April 9 pause and does not match the modeled event date.
narrow_corrected_title: Yale Budget Lab estimates tariff-related purchasing-power loss
narrow_corrected_claim: Yale Budget Lab estimated that the April 2 tariff package would reduce average household purchasing power by about $2,100; all tariffs then in effect were estimated at about $3,800.
exact_gap: Present the estimate as a model and identify which tariff package it covers; do not say consumers had already paid that amount or use $2,100 as the all-tariff total.

original_title: Trump Administration Proposes $800 Billion in Medicaid Cuts

sources.title: Budget of the United States Government, Fiscal Year 2018
sources.access_notes: GovInfo hosts the official FY2018 budget materials; the administration’s Medicaid proposal is about $610 billion in ten-year savings.

sources.title: Major Savings and Reforms, Budget of the U.S. Government, FY2018
sources.access_notes: Official budget detail identifies Medicaid reform savings and proposed per-capita-cap or block-grant structures.

sources.title: H.R. 1628, American Health Care Act of 2017
sources.access_notes: CBO score is a separate analysis of the House-passed bill; its Medicaid estimate must not be attributed to the administration budget.

supported_facts.fact: The May 2017 FY2018 administration budget proposed about $610 billion in Medicaid savings over ten years through Medicaid reforms, distinct from the separate ACA-replacement proposal.
CBO separately estimated roughly $834 billion in lower Medicaid outlays over ten years for the House-passed AHCA.

unsupported_original_claims: The May 23, 2017 administration budget itself proposed more than $800 billion in Medicaid cuts.
The House-passed AHCA estimate and the FY2018 budget savings estimate are the same proposal.
The cited sources establish that the AHCA passed the Senate or was enacted.
access_notes: The original combines the FY2018 budget’s roughly $610 billion Medicaid-savings proposal with CBO’s separate estimate for the House-passed AHCA. The cited budget document does not support an $800 billion Medicaid cut in the administration budget itself.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump FY2018 budget proposes about $610 billion in Medicaid savings
narrow_corrected_claim: Trump’s FY2018 budget proposed about $610 billion in Medicaid savings over ten years; the House-passed AHCA had a separate CBO estimate of about $834 billion in lower outlays.
exact_gap: Keep budget and legislation estimates separate, and describe proposed savings rather than enacted cuts. The source does not establish the other claims about AHCA coverage, rural hospitals, or Senate votes.

original_title: RFK Jr. Claims Autism Caused by Processed Food — No Scientific Evidence

sources.title: Health Secretary Kennedy says U.S. will know cause of autism “epidemic” by September
sources.access_notes: Reuters reports Kennedy’s timeline and the administration’s planned environmental-cause investigation in April 2025; it does not establish food, seed oils, or pesticides as causes.

supported_facts.fact: On April 10, 2025, Kennedy said the administration expected to identify a cause of the reported rise in autism diagnoses by September and described plans to investigate environmental factors.

unsupported_original_claims: Kennedy announced this initiative in March 2025.
Kennedy declared processed food, seed oils, and pesticides cause autism in this reported statement.
The announcement establishes a vaccine-autism claim or a scientific conclusion about causation.
access_notes: The cited Reuters report is dated April 10 and supports a promised timeline and environmental-cause investigation. It does not support the frozen record’s specific March date or its combined processed-food/seed-oil/pesticide causation claims.
narrow_corrected_title: Kennedy says HHS expects autism-cause findings by September
narrow_corrected_claim: Kennedy said in April 2025 that HHS expected to identify a cause of the rise in autism diagnoses by September and would investigate environmental factors.
exact_gap: Correct the month and attribute the forecast to Kennedy; source the specific dietary/pesticide claims separately or omit them.

original_title: Trump Bans Teaching of 'Divisive Concepts' in Federally Funded Schools

sources.title: Executive Order 14190: Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling
sources.access_notes: The order is dated January 29, 2025 and directs development of a strategy; the term “divisive concepts” belongs to a different 2020 order.

supported_facts.fact: Trump signed EO 14190 on January 29, 2025; it directs federal agencies to develop a strategy addressing what the order calls radical indoctrination in K-12 schooling.

unsupported_original_claims: The order was signed January 20, 2025.
EO 14190 defines “divisive concepts” using the text of EO 13950.
The order immediately prohibited the described curriculum nationwide or imposed the claimed funding conditions on universities.
Teachers’ reports, historian comparisons, and litigation warnings are established by this order.
access_notes: The relevant order is EO 14190, signed January 29, and framed as ending radical indoctrination in K-12 schooling. The frozen claim imports language from the separate 2020 EO 13950 and expands scope to universities and completed teaching bans.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump signs K-12 schooling order targeting alleged radical indoctrination
narrow_corrected_claim: EO 14190 directs a federal strategy targeting what the administration describes as radical indoctrination in K-12 schooling.
exact_gap: Correct the date and legal instrument; describe the order’s directive, not a nationwide completed ban, and omit the unrelated “divisive concepts” language unless separately documented.

original_title: Trump Signs Executive Order Cutting Funding to States That Comply With Court Orders Against Him

sources.title: Protecting American Communities from Criminal Aliens
sources.access_notes: The order directs identification of sanctuary jurisdictions and review of federal funding options; it does not say states are punished for complying with court orders.

supported_facts.fact: The April 2025 order directs agencies to identify sanctuary jurisdictions and federal funding that could be suspended or terminated where legally permitted, based on the administration’s view of obstruction to immigration enforcement.

unsupported_original_claims: The order targets states for complying with court orders against the administration.
The order itself immediately cut all federal funding to California, New York, and Illinois.
The source establishes that the governors immediately sued over the order.
access_notes: The order addresses jurisdictions the administration characterizes as obstructing immigration enforcement and calls for agencies to identify potential funding consequences. The source does not tie the action to compliance with court orders or document immediate across-the-board cuts.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump orders review of federal funds for sanctuary jurisdictions
narrow_corrected_claim: Trump’s April 2025 order directed agencies to identify sanctuary jurisdictions and federal funds that might be suspended or terminated under existing law.
exact_gap: Remove the claim that funding was threatened for obeying judicial orders; preserve the limited sanctuary-jurisdiction directive and its conditional/legal constraints.

original_title: Trump Ends Affirmative Action in All Federally Funded Institutions

sources.title: Executive Order 14173: Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity
sources.access_notes: The order was signed January 21, 2025, revokes EO 11246’s federal-contractor requirements, and directs federal agencies to enforce civil-rights laws; it is not a blanket repeal at all federally funded institutions.

supported_facts.fact: EO 14173, signed January 21, 2025, revoked prior federal-contractor affirmative-action requirements and directed changes to federal contracting and grant-related enforcement.

unsupported_original_claims: Trump ended every affirmative-action, outreach, pipeline, and mentorship program at all federally funded institutions on January 20.
The order directly covers all universities, hospitals, nonprofits, and state agencies in the sweeping manner stated.
The source establishes that any institution maintaining a diversity initiative would automatically lose funding.
access_notes: The order was signed January 21 and is directed at federal-contractor rules, agency enforcement, and grant-related conditions. It does not establish an immediate blanket prohibition on all affirmative-action practices across every federally funded institution.
narrow_corrected_claim: EO 14173 revoked federal-contractor affirmative-action requirements and directed federal agencies to address what the administration characterized as illegal discrimination and DEI.
exact_gap: Correct the date and scope; do not say all federally funded institutions’ outreach, mentoring, or admissions programs were abolished by this order.

original_title: Trump Ends All Federal Arts and Humanities Funding — NEA and NEH Abolished

sources.title: NEA grant recipients receive rejection and rescission notices under Trump administration
sources.access_notes: AP reports the FY2026 budget proposal, grant disruptions, and staffing actions; it does not report that Congress-created agencies were abolished.

supported_facts.fact: The Trump administration’s proposed FY2026 budget sought to eliminate the National Endowment for the Arts, and AP reported grant rejection/rescission notices and staff departures in May 2025.

unsupported_original_claims: NEA and NEH were legally abolished in March 2025.
All federal arts and humanities funding ended or every affected community lost support.
The source establishes the claimed simultaneous elimination of the Institute of Museum and Library Services.
access_notes: AP documents a proposed budget elimination and grant disruptions, not abolition of the congressionally created NEA/NEH. This article does not substantiate the claims about all federal funding, IMLS, combined budgets, or nationwide community impacts.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump budget proposes eliminating NEA amid grant disruptions
narrow_corrected_claim: The FY2026 budget proposed eliminating the NEA, while grant notices and staffing changes disrupted some arts funding in 2025.
exact_gap: Describe the proposal and specific grant actions; do not describe either agency or all federal arts/humanities support as abolished.

sources.access_notes: Contemporaneous reporting describes foreign business interests and ethics concerns.

supported_facts.fact: Washington Post reporting documented Trump-branded or licensing relationships, including projects in India, the Philippines, and Turkey, and described ethics experts’ conflict-of-interest concerns while Trump held office.

unsupported_original_claims: The three governments paid Trump directly through those projects.
Specific U.S. policy concessions were exchanged for the business relationships in each country.

original_title: Trump targets pro-Palestinian organizations as terrorist-adjacent

sources.title: Recent Actions: June 10, 2025
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of the Treasury, OFAC
sources.access_notes: OFAC lists specific designated entities and grounds stated by Treasury; the notice is not a blanket designation of pro-Palestinian advocacy groups.

sources.title: U.S. issues sanctions against charities supporting Hamas, PFLP
sources.access_notes: Reuters reports the June 10 sanctions and attributes the alleged militant links to U.S. officials.

supported_facts.fact: On June 10, 2025, Treasury announced sanctions against specific organizations, including Palestinian group Addameer, alleging links/support for designated militant groups.

unsupported_original_claims: The Trump administration designated pro-Palestinian advocacy organizations generally as terrorist-adjacent in March.
The sources establish tax-status threats or prosecutions of members solely for protected political speech.
The allegations against every named entity are independently proven by the sanctions announcement.
access_notes: The sources document a June 10 action against named entities based on administration allegations, not a March blanket policy targeting pro-Palestinian advocacy or protected speech. Treasury’s stated allegations are not independent findings of guilt.
narrow_corrected_title: Treasury sanctions specific organizations over alleged militant links
narrow_corrected_claim: Treasury sanctioned specific Palestinian and other organizations on June 10, 2025, alleging links to designated militant groups.

original_title: Trump executive order designating certain protest groups as domestic terrorists

sources.title: Designating Antifa as a Domestic Terrorist Organization
sources.access_notes: The September 22, 2025 order labels Antifa and directs use of existing authorities against illegal operations; it does not itself criminalize all nonviolent protest.

sources.title: Trump signs order designating antifa as a domestic terrorist organization
sources.access_notes: AP reports the order and legal questions about applying a domestic-terror label; it does not document a wave of prosecutions resulting from it.

supported_facts.fact: Trump signed an order on September 22, 2025 labeling Antifa a domestic terrorist organization and directing agencies to investigate and disrupt illegal operations attributed to its adherents.
The order does not create a statutory domestic designation system or itself criminalize peaceful protest; AP coverage describes legal and constitutional questions about its effect.

unsupported_original_claims: The relevant order was signed in March 2025.
The order formally designated multiple protest organizations.
The order criminalized nonviolent political dissent or caused a wave of terrorism prosecutions.
access_notes: The documented order was issued in September and refers to Antifa, not a list of protest groups. Its directive concerns illegal operations under existing authorities; neither the order nor the cited AP report shows that peaceful protest itself became criminal or that the asserted prosecution wave followed.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump signs order labeling Antifa a domestic terrorist organization
narrow_corrected_claim: On September 22, 2025, Trump signed an order labeling Antifa a domestic terrorist organization and directing agencies to address alleged illegal operations under existing law.
exact_gap: Correct the date and singular scope. Do not describe the order as criminalizing nonviolent activity or causing prosecutions without specific case evidence.
